title: How the Iran War Exposed China's New Oil Weapon: Clean Energy Dominance
excerpt: As the Strait of Hormuz closure disrupts global crude supplies, China's EV boom and clean tech exports are reshaping energy geopolitics — with major implications for India.
body:
• China's clean energy exports hit a record $26 billion in March 2026 after the Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, cutting roughly 10 million barrels per day of crude supply
  • Chinese passenger EV and hybrid exports now account for 53 percent of all vehicle exports, up more than 100 percent year-over-year, with battery exports reaching $10 billion in a single month
  • India faces a dual squeeze — higher oil import costs from the Hormuz disruption and growing dependence on Chinese clean tech, from solar panels to EV batteries

The U.S. and Israeli war against Iran, now in its fifth month, has produced an unexpected winner in global energy markets: China's clean technology industry.

The closure of the Strait of Hormuz — the narrow waterway through which roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas passes — has sent crude prices above $103 a barrel and triggered fuel shortages across Southeast Asia. But while traditional energy importers scramble for alternatives, China has positioned itself as both a buyer of discounted crude and the world's leading supplier of the technology to move beyond fossil fuels entirely.

The $26 Billion Month

In March 2026, Chinese exports of batteries, solar panels, electric vehicles and other clean energy components totalled $26 billion, according to data compiled by clean tech think tank Ember. That was the highest monthly tally ever recorded and represented a 52 percent increase over the same month in 2025.

Battery systems led the surge at just over $10 billion in sales, compared with a monthly average of $7 billion since the start of 2025. Europe absorbed 43 percent of Chinese battery exports, with Germany alone importing $1.26 billion worth. Solar exports more than doubled from February, reaching $4.8 billion, with 50 countries setting all-time records for Chinese solar imports in a single month.

"The Iranian energy crisis is going to turbo charge the global energy transition away from oil and gas from the Middle East and a pivot to clean technologies — wind, solar, electric vehicles — that China is a very significant leader on."

— Li Shuo, Director, Asia Society Policy Institute's China Climate Hub

EVs as Strategic Shield

China's rapid EV adoption has served as a strategic buffer against the oil shock. More than half of all new vehicle sales in the country are now battery-powered, and Chinese passenger EV and hybrid exports surged to 53 percent of all vehicle exports — more than doubling in a year, according to the China Passenger Car Association.

The country's oil stockpiles now exceed those of the United States, and its installed wind and solar capacity leads the world. In 2025, China added roughly half of all global wind and solar energy, according to the Global Energy Monitor.

"Fossil fuels are unstable" compared with clean energy, and "buying Chinese products that get you off the fossil fuel freight train provides more stable electricity than any other source," said Jon B. Alterman, chair in Global Security and Geostrategy at the Center for Strategic and International Studies.

India's Double Bind

For India, the situation presents a strategic dilemma. As the world's third-largest oil importer, the country is heavily exposed to the Hormuz disruption and the resulting price spikes. India was among the top five buyers of Chinese solar panels in March, alongside Indonesia, the Philippines and Pakistan.

The Iran war has accelerated EV adoption across South Asia, with two- and three-wheeler electric sales expected to see a compound annual growth rate of 30 percent, according to Fastmarkets. Vietnam's VinFast, which now operates plants in India and Indonesia, has grown from 7,000 EV sales in 2022 to 197,000 in 2025.

But greater reliance on Chinese clean tech creates its own dependency. The manufacture of EV batteries depends on sulphuric acid, a key component in extracting nickel and lithium, and about half of global seaborne sulphur passed through the Strait of Hormuz before the conflict. Volumes through the strait have collapsed, according to commodity analysts Kpler, with only 30,000 metric tons making it out in April.

A Shifting Energy Order

"From China's perspective, the world is shifting from one in which energy supply security is based on physical resources, to a world in which it's based on technology. And that's a world that's very well suited to us," said Erica Downs, who studies Chinese energy markets at Columbia University's Center on Global Energy Policy.

Gulf Arab states, frustrated by the limits of American power in the conflict, are now looking to Beijing to use its economic leverage over Iran to reopen the strait. China's Foreign Minister Wang Yi has held dozens of calls with counterparts seeking a ceasefire, while special envoy Zhai Jun has visited Gulf capitals and Tehran.

For the Indian diaspora watching these shifts, the implications run deep. India's energy security calculus is being rewritten in real time — caught between expensive crude, Chinese clean tech, and the strategic question of whether accelerating its own renewable transition is the only path to true energy independence.
